newsitem.title: USA: Dollar ends U.S. trade higher on strong economy.
newsitem.headline: Dollar ends U.S. trade higher on strong economy.

text.p: The dollar closed higher against most major currencies, bolstered by hopes for higher U.S. short-term interest rates and enthusiasm for an agreement to balance the federal budget in five years, experts said.

With no key economic data released on Monday, experts looked partly to a labor market report issued on Friday for signs the Federal Reserve may tighten credit again when it meet on May 20 to keep the economy from growing too rapidly.
The report showed the economy added a less-than-expected 142,000 jobs in April, but the April unemployment rate fell to 4.9 percent, the lowest level since 1973.
Fed policymakers had boosted the federal funds rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 percent on March 25.
"I would be very surprised if they didn't raise (rates) in May," said Stephen Jury, chief dealer of foreign exchange at Union Bank of Switzerland.
Jury said the recent gains in the stock market give the Fed "even more confidence to go ahead and hike rates."
The Dow Jones industrials scored a record high on Monday, soaring 143 points or two percent to finish at 7214.
The dollar finished at 1.7325/35 marks, up from 1.7285/90 marks at the open.
The dollar finished at 126.58/63 yen, up from 126.38/48 yen at the open.
The federal budget deal announced last Friday also remained in the spotlight amid a dearth of economic data on Monday.

The budget plan included a net tax cut of $85 billion, but a major part of the savings required to shrink the deficit would be found in the Medicare health care program for the elderly, which would see a $115 billion reduction.
Cuts in taxes and spending would be spread out over five years.

"I think the feeling with the U.S. is, especially in the short-term anyway, it's been helpful to the dollar because it's spread out over such a long period of time that it's not going to provide much of a retard to U.S. economic growth," said John Rothfield, an international economist at Nationsbanc.
"It'll free up some resources for higher private sector growth," Rothfield added.
Traders played down the importance of dollar gains on Monday as financial markets in Tokyo and London were closed because of holidays.
Markets in Tokyo were closed for the Children's Day holiday, and Britons enjoyed a bank holiday on Monday. Trading in Tokyo and London will resume on Tuesday.
Not surprisingly, traders described volume in the foreign exchange market on Monday as very light and warned movements in exchange rates could be magnified.
"With two of the major three treasury centers closed for the day, any move should be exaggerated," said Doug Lee, an assistant vice president of foreign exchange at Sakura Bank Ltd in New York.
Elsewhere, the dollar closed at 1.4740/50 Swiss francs, up from 1.4715/25 francs at the open.
The pound rose to $1.6225/35 from $1.6203/13.
The dollar slid to Canadian $1.3790/95 from C$1.3815/20.
The Australian dollar ended at $0.7805/10, up from $0.7802/07.
